confidence_note: Checked against the book text (Part II, Howard Hughes chapter). Old text claims dropped: hotel-room seclusion, long nails, dehydration, Holiday asking when success is most dangerous. Numbers keep the book scope.
facts: Jan 1924: Hughes Sr. died of a heart attack at a business meeting, aged 54; son, 18, inherited three quarters of the tool company (patents and leases critical to oil drilling, worth nearly $1 million).
Still a legal minor, he leveraged personal assets and nearly all company funds to buy out relatives who objected; it later yielded billions in cash profit over the next century.
He left Houston, never entered HQ again, used it as cash source; moved to LA to be producer and celebrity.
Lost over $8M trading stocks from bed before the Depression; Hell's Angels took 3 years, lost $1.5M on a $4.2M budget; $4M lost on Chrysler stock early 1930.
Two WWII defense contracts worth $40M failed; Spruce Goose: 5+ years, about $20M, one flight of barely a mile at 70 ft; hangar in Long Beach at $1M a year for decades.
RKO lost over $22M, staff from 2,000 to under 500; when he handed defense contracting to executives it began to thrive, in Holiday's words because of his absence.
A bad businessman usually fails and vanishes; Hughes stayed afloat on father's company profits so the damage is visible.

Biographers: sat naked in white chair, unwashed, dictating a memo on Kleenex then a brilliant strategy; IBM two-subsidiaries comparison. Near death an aide praised his life; he replied swapping places would be regretted within a week.
scene_details: Spruce Goose hangar at $1M a year
tension: Gifted and brave, he wasted it, and only a rich father's company let the damage stay visible.
opening_idea: Start from one concrete image such as the white chair, the Spruce Goose hangar or the Hell's Angels numbers.

lessons.idea: Check how the work runs without you.
lessons.anchor: Hughes's defense business began to thrive once he handed it to executives.
lessons.everyday_example_idea: A tailor who approves every order takes two days off and reads the order book.

reflect_final: Which task are you keeping in your own hands mainly because letting go would make you feel less important?

use_cases.situation: You approve everything on your team.
use_cases.move: Hand two decisions to the team, citing the defense business that recovered after Hughes handed it off.

use_cases.situation: A promoted friend does everything alone.
use_cases.move: Ask what happens if they step back from a project for a week.

use_cases.situation: After a good run you feel sure about a big call.
use_cases.move: Ask who could tell you no before deciding alone.

pocket_idea: Hand one task away for a week and watch what happens.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: Hughes's defense business only began to thrive after he handed it off.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: Hughes inherited the company at 18, lost fortunes on films, stocks, a plane that flew once and a studio; the defense arm did better once he let go. Holiday: ego wrecked him.
